title: 'The virgin will be with child'
summary: Isaiah's sign to King Ahaz, a child named Immanuel, is read by Matthew as fulfilled in the birth of Jesus. Hebrew ʿalmah means a young woman of marriageable age; the Greek Septuagint Matthew quotes uses parthenos, 'virgin'.

sources.title: Septuagint Isaiah 7:14 (παρθένος)
sources.note: the translation Matthew quotes, 2nd c. BC

sources.title: Strong's H5959 עַלְמָה
sources.note: 'a lass (as veiled or private)'; also Gen 24:43, Exod 2:8

traditions: Christian traditions read it as messianic; Jewish tradition reads it of a child in Ahaz's day (Hezekiah or Isaiah's son); many Christian scholars hold both — a near fulfilment and a fuller one

title: A ruler from Bethlehem
summary: The chief priests cite Micah to Herod as the settled expectation that the Messiah would come from Bethlehem; John 7:42 shows the crowd knew it too.

title: 'Out of Egypt I called My Son'
summary: In Hosea the 'son' is Israel at the Exodus. Matthew applies it to the child's return from Egypt — a typological fulfilment: Jesus re-lives Israel's story.

sources.title: The Use of the Old Testament in St. Matthew's Gospel
sources.author: Robert H. Gundry

traditions: Typological reading standard across Christian traditions; not a prediction in its Hosea context

title: Rachel weeping for her children
summary: Jeremiah pictures Rachel mourning the exiles marched past Ramah; Matthew hears the same cry over Bethlehem's children. Rachel's tomb was traditionally near Bethlehem (Genesis 35:19).

title: A voice in the wilderness
summary: All four Gospels apply Isaiah's herald of return from exile to John the Baptist; John applies it to himself. The Qumran community used the same verse for its own desert vocation (1QS 8:13-14).

sources.title: Community Rule (1QS) 8:13–14
sources.note: Dead Sea Scrolls; the sect 'goes into the wilderness to prepare the way'

title: 'I will send My messenger'
summary: Jesus identifies John as the messenger of Malachi 3:1 (and, in Matthew 11:14, as the Elijah of Malachi 4:5).

title: Light in Galilee of the nations
summary: Matthew reads Jesus' move to Capernaum, in the old tribal lands of Zebulun and Naphtali, as the dawning Isaiah promised for the region first overrun by Assyria.

title: 'He took on our infirmities'
summary: Matthew applies the Servant's bearing of sickness to Jesus' healings; Philip explains the same chapter to the Ethiopian as being about Jesus.
traditions: Christian traditions: the Servant is the Messiah; Jewish tradition since the medieval period commonly reads the Servant as Israel; the Great Isaiah Scroll (c. 125 BC) shows the text was fixed before either reading

title: Your king comes on a donkey
summary: Jesus stages the entry to Jerusalem to match Zechariah's humble king; Matthew and John both say so explicitly.

title: The stone the builders rejected
summary: Jesus applies the psalm to himself at the end of the parable of the tenants; Peter repeats it before the Sanhedrin.

title: 'Sit at My right hand'
summary: The most-quoted Old Testament verse in the New Testament. Jesus uses it to ask how the Messiah can be both David's son and David's Lord.

title: Thirty pieces of silver thrown to the potter
summary: Matthew attributes the quotation to Jeremiah, though its wording is Zechariah's; Jeremiah 19 and 32 supply the potter and the field. Ancient citation practice often named the more prominent prophet of a combined quotation.

title: They divided My garments
summary: John quotes the psalm directly at the crucifixion; Jesus' cry from the cross (Matthew 27:46) is its opening line.

title: 'They will look on the One they have pierced'
summary: John applies Zechariah's mourning for 'the one they pierced' to the spear-thrust; Revelation universalises it.

title: 'I will pour out My Spirit on all people'
summary: Peter's first words at Pentecost: 'this is what was spoken by the prophet Joel'.

title: Seventy years for Babylon
summary: Jeremiah's seventy years of Babylonian domination; the Chronicler and Ezra say Cyrus's decree (539 BC) fulfilled it, and Daniel counts on it. From Nebuchadnezzar's first campaign (605 BC) to 539 is 66 years; from the temple's destruction (586) to its rededication (516) is 70.

sources.title: Cyrus Cylinder (BM 90920) and the Nabonidus Chronicle (BM 35382)
sources.note: fix the fall of Babylon to 539 BC
